# BirdNET v03：鳥與森林場景

## wood-borer-larva-v01.png

Create a realistic close-up macro nature photograph for a public ecology explainer, wide horizontal 16:9 frame. A single cream-colored wood-boring beetle larva in a naturally opened narrow gallery just beneath a loose flake of bark on a dead conifer trunk. Show a soft segmented grub with a small amber-brown head, believable anatomy, no prominent caterpillar legs, on pale weathered wood with fine sawdust and winding shallow gallery grooves. The bark is dark, rough and locally charred at the outer edge, but this is after a past fire, not burning now. The photo should make it clear why a dead standing tree can hold food for a woodpecker. The larva occupies only about a quarter of the frame width, centered, complete body visible; surrounding real wood and bark remain prominent. Soft natural daylight, fine physical texture, restrained brown and cream colors, documentary macro photography. No cutaway diagram, no transparent wood, no labels, scale bars, rulers, text, arrows, humans, tools, birds or giant fantasy insects. No injury. New generated teaching image, not research data.

## forest-mosaic-v01.png

Create a realistic documentary landscape photograph for a public ecology explainer, wide cinematic 16:9 composition, high resolution. A mid-distance ground-to-hillside view of a Sierra Nevada mixed conifer forest several growing seasons after a patchy wildfire. The forest visibly contains a natural mosaic: on the left healthy mature green pines and firs with layered canopy, toward the middle and right a small patch of standing dead partly charred trunks, some unburned live green trees among them and low regrowth. A believable mountain forest, not a symmetrical split screen, no sharp artificial boundary. Soft overcast late afternoon light, restrained deep greens and charcoal browns, detailed natural bark and needles, readable subtle detail in shadows rather than crushed blacks. The camera is among living trees, looking into the forest and across a small slope; not a drone map or distant panorama. The dead trees remain clearly visible and recognizable as standing forest structure. No flames, smoke, people, vehicles, machines, buildings, text, labels, diagrams, charts, overlays or decorative symbols. This is a photographic teaching scene, not a recreation of a documented study site. Keep the central 60 percent useful for a vertical crop.

## spotted-owl-forest-v01.png

Create a highly realistic wildlife documentary photograph, horizontal 16:9 frame, for a public ecology explainer. Subject: a California spotted owl, Strix occidentalis occidentalis, perched naturally on a thick weathered branch beside the massive trunk of a mature conifer in a Sierra Nevada mixed-conifer forest. Show the entire owl including feet and tail, clearly identifiable at roughly one third of frame height. Anatomically accurate rounded head WITHOUT ear tufts, large very dark brown almost black eyes, soft brown facial disk with subtle pale rings, medium brown plumage scattered with cream-white spots on the head and back, brown-and-cream mottled horizontal spotting below, not the vertical streaked chest of a barred owl. It faces slightly toward camera. The owl is near the middle, slightly right, so it remains present in a vertical crop. Show substantial living-tree canopy, branches and shaded forest behind it; the forest is a visible home, not an isolated portrait on a blurry void. Believable scale: the old tree trunk is much wider than the owl. Cool deep green forest with soft natural shaded late-afternoon light and fine plumage texture, editorial nature photography, no dramatic fantasy lighting. Calm stationary pose. No humans, equipment, fires, other birds, text, infographic, labels or logos. A new generated teaching scene, not a purported field-study photograph.

## black-backed-woodpecker-v01.png

Create a highly realistic wildlife documentary photograph, horizontal 16:9 frame, for a public ecology explainer. A single adult male black-backed woodpecker (Picoides arcticus) clinging vertically to a standing dead conifer trunk in a patchily burned Sierra Nevada forest, seen in clean three-quarter side view. The bird is inspecting a small naturally flaked patch of bark with its bill near the wood, not in exaggerated motion. Show the complete body, natural feet gripping bark and stiff tail braced against the trunk. Anatomically accurate medium-small woodpecker: solid glossy black BACK without a white dorsal stripe, mostly black head, small yellow crown patch (NOT red), a single white moustache stripe, pale whitish underside with dark barred flanks, straight stout dark bill. The bird sits near center of frame, roughly 35 percent of frame height, entire shape identifiable and suitable for a vertical crop. Richly textured charred and weathered bark, small exposed pale wood patch and a few natural chips at the bill; do not display oversized insects or a cutaway diagram. In the clearly recognizable background are standing dead trees mixed with surviving live green conifers and modest understory regrowth, no active fire or smoke. Soft natural daylight, restrained charcoal and deep forest green, detailed photographic textures, no painted or cartoon appearance. No extra limbs, duplicate birds, red crest, white back stripe, humans, instruments, text, labels, charts or logos. This is a generated natural-history teaching scene, not an original research photograph.
